questions.q: What are the two specific substances present in the environment that must react with iron to cause rusting?
questions.a: The two substances are oxygen (from air) and water (from moisture). A wrong answer suggests the student is guessing common environmental factors (like dust or sunlight) rather than identifying the specific chemical reactants needed for oxidation.

questions.q: Why is the formation of rust considered a "chemical change" rather than a "physical change"?
questions.a: It is a chemical change because a new substance (iron oxide) is formed with different properties, and the process cannot be reversed by simple means. A wrong answer suggests the student believes the change is merely in shape or appearance, missing the fact that the material itself has changed composition.

questions.q: If you have a block of pure iron and it turns into rust, what happens to its ability to stick to a magnet?
questions.a: The block will lose its ability to stick to a magnet because rust is non-magnetic. A wrong answer indicates the student has not grasped that the physical properties of the material (magnetism) change when the chemical structure changes.

questions.q: Compare the physical appearance of iron and rust.
questions.a: Iron is grey, hard, and strong, whereas rust is reddish-brown, brittle, and weak. A wrong answer reveals confusion between the original metal and the product of the reaction.

questions.q: If an iron rod is kept in a vacuum (an area with no air or moisture), will it rust? Explain why.
questions.a: No, it will not rust because the necessary reactants (oxygen and water) are absent. This tests the student's ability to apply the conditions of the chemical change to a hypothetical scenario.

questions.q: Design an experiment to prove that moisture is necessary for iron to rust.
questions.a: Place one iron nail in a dry container and one in a container with water/moisture, then observe which one changes over a week. A poor answer fails to include a "control" (the dry nail) to compare against, showing a lack of scientific methodology.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Rusting is a chemical change where iron reacts with oxygen and moisture from the air to form a new ______ called iron oxide (rust).
Fill in the blank: Have you ever noticed how the iron gate in your garden or a bicycle left in the rain turns a ______-brown color over time?
What is Rusting? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Rusting is a chemical change where iron reacts with oxygen and moisture from the air to form a new substance called iron oxide (rust).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Rusting?
questions.a: Students often believe that rusting is just "dirt" or "stains" that can be wiped off, or that it is a physical change like melting ice.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify rusting as a chemical change by contrasting the physical properties of iron (grey, hard, magnetic) with those of rust (reddish-brown, brittle, non-magnetic) and listing the two necessary conditions (oxygen and water).
